text: Cloud providers don't run one giant, undifferentiated datacenter somewhere — they operate a deliberate, structured hierarchy of regions and availability zones, and understanding exactly how that hierarchy works is what actually lets you build something resilient instead of just hoping nothing ever breaks.

A region is a large geographic area, like AWS's us-east-1 in Northern Virginia or Azure's eastus, where a provider runs a whole cluster of datacenters close enough together for fast connections, but far enough apart to be independently resilient. Inside every region are multiple availability zones, or AZs for short — physically separate facilities, each with its own independent power supply, cooling system, and network connectivity, specifically so that a problem in one AZ can't reach any of the others.

Here's why that separation actually matters in practice: an e-commerce site runs two web servers behind a load balancer, one in us-east-1a, one in us-east-1b. A power failure takes down the datacenter behind 1a entirely. The load balancer detects that the first server has gone unhealthy and routes all of the traffic over to the server in 1b instead — customers never notice a single thing went wrong. If both servers had been placed in 1a alone, the entire site would have gone down right along with that one facility.

That's the real, practical difference between multi-AZ and multi-region design. Spreading your resources across multiple availability zones within one region is the low-cost baseline that essentially every production workload should have as a matter of course. Spreading across multiple regions entirely is a much bigger step — it protects against a whole regional disaster and can reduce latency for a genuinely global user base, but it comes with real added cost and real added complexity.

That closes out cloud computing fundamentals. Next up, Chapter 7: virtual networks — VPCs in AWS and VNets in Azure — where you'll learn to build your own private network inside the cloud, on top of exactly the regions and availability zones you just learned about here.
